query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, intermediate-temperature aging induces the formation of nanoscale clusters of solute elements (primarily Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries. These nanoclusters reduce the local cohesive strength of the grain boundaries, predisposing them to intergranular crack initiation under mechanical stress, and thereby drive a ductile-to-brittle transition that is mechanistically distinct from conventional grain-boundary precipitation mechanisms.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, single-phase equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with a face-centered cubic (FCC) structure exhibiting homogeneous composition and ductile behavior.
generation.intervention: Subject specimens to controlled aging treatments at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 250–350 °C) for carefully determined durations in a high-vacuum or inert atmosphere to promote nanocluster formation at grain boundaries without causing significant grain growth or bulk phase decomposition. Enhanced real-time monitoring methods (such as in situ diffraction or small-angle scattering) will be employed to fine-tune the aging window.
generation.conditions: Conduct constant-strain-rate tensile tests at room temperature and at intermediate service temperatures (e.g., 200–300 °C). Compare the mechanical behavior of as-cast (baseline) versus aged specimens. Use high-resolution microscopy and atom probe tomography (APT) to evaluate the grain boundary chemistry and to confirm the presence and morphology of the nanoclusters.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoscale solute clusters (particularly rich in Cr, Ni, and Mn) localized along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The nanoclusters act as local defects that reduce grain boundary cohesion, thereby providing easy nucleation sites for intergranular cracks under mechanical loading. This mechanism promotes a brittle failure mode as opposed to the more uniformly distributed plastic deformation observed in the as-cast alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Aged samples are expected to show a measurable reduction in toughness (evidenced by lower fracture strains and premature intergranular cracking) relative to the as-cast baseline. Microstructural analysis should reveal the presence of nanoscale solute clusters at the grain boundaries in the aged specimens, confirming the hypothesized embrittlement mechanism. This effect should be prominent under moderate plastic deformation conditions and distinguishable from the behavior observed in conventional alloys.
generation.baseline: The untreated, as-cast CrMnFeCoNi HEA, which exhibits uniform, ductile deformation behavior characterized by transgranular fracture and absence of detectable nanocluster formation at grain boundaries.
generation.boundary: The proposed mechanism is expected to be relevant under intermediate temperature conditions and moderate strain rates where thermally activated diffusion is sufficient to enable nanocluster formation but not so high as to initiate alternative mechanisms (e.g., adiabatic shear or extensive precipitation). At very low temperatures or extremely high strain rates, other deformation mechanisms may dominate.
generation.uncertainty: There is some uncertainty regarding the precise kinetics and spatial distribution of nanocluster formation within the narrow aging window. The risk exists that slight deviations in the aging parameters might trigger broader precipitate formation or grain coarsening, which would confound the intended test of the nanoclustering-induced brittleness mechanism.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA specimens: one set of as-cast samples and one set subjected to the intermediate-temperature aging treatment under optimized conditions. Conduct constant-strain-rate tensile tests at room temperature and at intermediate service temperatures. Concurrently, utilize atom probe tomography (APT) and high-resolution TEM to document the chemical state and structure at the grain boundaries.
measurements: Fracture strain and toughness from tensile tests
Fracture surface morphology (intergranular vs. transgranular fracture)
Presence, size, and distribution of nanoscale solute clusters at grain boundaries via APT/HR-TEM
Comparison of grain size and overall microstructural integrity between as-cast and aged samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aged samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in toughness and fracture strain compared to the as-cast baseline, or if microstructural characterization fails to detect the formation of nanoscale solute clusters at the grain boundaries (with no significant difference from the as-cast state), then the hypothesis that nanoclustering-induced GB embrittlement is the primary mechanism for brittle behavior will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

In addition, the segregation of trace elements C and B into GBs is beneficial to improve GB cohesion as long as M6C carbides do not precipitate (, ). The 1D compositional profiles in fig. S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. proposals.material_system: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase, FCC) with equiatomic composition
proposals.intervention: Systematically age samples at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 250–350 °C) for controlled durations to induce potential grain boundary nanoclustering without triggering significant grain coarsening or bulk phase segregation
proposals.conditions: Specimens to be aged in high-vacuum or inert atmosphere to avoid oxidation; post-aging, perform constant-strain-rate tensile tests at room and intermediate temperatures (e.g., 200–300 °C) to assess toughness and ductility relative to as-cast baseline
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation of nanoclusters of solute elements (e.g., Cr, Ni, Mn) at grain boundaries that decrease cohesive strength without invoking conventional intermetallic precipitation
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that even in a single-phase HEA, kinetic driving forces at intermediate temperatures promote subtle elemental clustering at GBs that reduces intergranular cohesion, leading to a ductile-to-brittle transition distinct from grain-boundary segregation in conventional alloys
proposals.predicted_outcome: Aged samples should show a measurable reduction in toughness (increased intergranular cracking on fracture surfaces and lower fracture strains) relative to the baseline, with atom probe tomography (APT) confirming the presence of nanoscale clusters at GBs. This transition would be prominent under service loads that create moderate plastic deformation but not under very high or cryogenic strain rates where other mechanisms dominate
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It directly tests whether subtle, thermally induced nanoclustering at grain boundaries—a departure from conventional coarse precipitation—governs toughness degradation in a compositionally complex HEA, thereby distinguishing the HEA behavior from that of conventional alloys

proposals.material_system: Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (retained single-phase FCC) with controlled chemical homogeneity
proposals.intervention: Perform controlled low-temperature annealing treatments (e.g., 600–750 °C for varying times) designed to trigger local chemical ordering along grain boundaries without causing overall phase separation or significant grain growth
proposals.conditions: Anneal samples in a reducing atmosphere to prevent oxidation; compare specimens that undergo the treatment with as-cast, unannealed counterparts; employ high-resolution TEM and diffraction methods to detect localized B2 or ordered clusters preferentially at GBs
proposals.structural_mediator: Locally ordered (incipient intermetallic-like) clusters forming along GBs that act as cohesion-lowering features interrupting dislocation continuity
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that under certain thermal exposures, even a single-phase HEA can undergo localized short-range ordering (akin to B2 or other incipient intermetallic structures) at grain boundaries, thereby creating brittle paths that facilitate intergranular cracking despite otherwise homogeneous microstructure
proposals.predicted_outcome: Annealed samples are expected to exhibit reduced ductility and toughness with clear microscopic evidence of local ordered clusters at GBs, contrasting with the uniform deformation seen in as-cast samples. Tests under moderate-to-high service temperatures (up to ~750 °C) should reveal a distinct drop in fracture strain, with such features absent in conventional alloys that undergo full precipitation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It offers a controlled comparison based on thermal activation of local ordering, testing whether incipient ordering at GBs in a compositionally complex system can reproduce brittle behavior, separate from the classical segregation or coarse precipitate mechanism seen in conventional alloys

proposals.material_system: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy with ultra-fine grains (initial single-phase FCC)
proposals.intervention: Subject specimens to high strain-rate deformation tests (using split-Hopkinson bar or high-speed compression/tension setups) at ambient and moderately low temperatures to induce transient adiabatic heating and extreme local strain gradients
proposals.conditions: Conduct tests at a range of strain rates (10^2 to 10^3 s⁻¹) and temperatures (room temperature down to cryogenic, e.g., 77 K) to map the deformation response; use post-deformation microscopy (e.g., SEM/TEM) to detect formation of shear bands, localized nanovoid formation, and grain-boundary decohesion features
proposals.structural_mediator: Localized adiabatic shear bands and associated nanovoiding phenomena at grain boundaries, enhanced by the severe lattice distortion inherent to high-entropy systems
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that under rapid loading, the kinetic energy and local adiabatic heating lead to pronounced strain localization along grain boundaries. This, superimposed on lattice distortion effects, triggers the nucleation of microvoids and microcracks that coalesce to form brittle fracture paths, a mechanism distinct from slower diffusion-mediated segregation
proposals.predicted_outcome: High strain-rate tests should reveal a transition to brittle behavior (decreased ductility and premature intergranular fracture) with microstructural evidence of shear band-induced voids along GBs, in contrast to the more homogeneous plastic flow at lower strain rates. The critical strain rate for embrittlement will delineate service boundaries
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It distinguishes the mechanistic origin of brittleness in HEAs under dynamic service loads from conventional alloys where grain-boundary precipitation dominates, thereby testing a rate-dependent, adiabatic shear mechanism that emerges primarily in compositionally complex systems

proposals.material_system: AlCoCrFeNiMo0.25 high-entropy alloy with a controlled level of impurities
proposals.intervention: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) ultra-high purity HEA minimizing interstitial impurities (oxygen, nitrogen) and (b) HEA intentionally doped with trace amounts of oxygen via controlled atmosphere processing; then, subject both sets to identical mechanical testing
proposals.conditions: Manufacture alloys by arc melting under high vacuum for the pure variant and under a slightly oxygenated environment for the doped variant; perform tensile and fracture toughness tests at ambient and elevated temperatures (up to 650 °C) to simulate demanding engineering service conditions
proposals.structural_mediator: Impurity-induced segregation at grain boundaries that promotes local embrittlement by reducing the cohesive strength, even in the absence of large-scale intermetallic precipitation
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that trace interstitial impurities, even in a compositionally complex and nominally single-phase HEA, can preferentially segregate to grain boundaries. This segregation undermines GB cohesion and becomes the nucleation point for brittle fracture, a mechanism parallel yet distinguishable from classical precipitation effects in conventional alloys
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the high-purity baseline, oxygen-doped HEA samples will display a significant reduction in toughness and ductility, with fracture surfaces showing intergranular decohesion. Conversely, if toughness degradation is not observed or impurities do not preferentially locate at GBs, the hypothesis would be falsified
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: It provides a controlled comparison that directly tests whether impurity-driven grain boundary weakening—a known effect in refractory and conventional alloys—also governs brittle behavior in compositionally complex HEAs, thereby challenging the expectation that HEAs are inherently resistant to such embrittlement

critiques.addresses_problem: The approach directly tests a mechanistic hypothesis for toughness degradation by probing a dynamic, strain-rate‐dependent adiabatic shear band mechanism that is distinct from conventional diffusion‐mediated grain boundary precipitation.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the constraint by using a compositionally complex, single‐phase CoCrFeMnNi HEA with ultra‐fine grains and retains the alloy system while exploring dynamic deformation at ambient and cryogenic temperatures.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism is physically sound; rapid deformation can induce local adiabatic heating and shear band formation that would promote nanovoiding and intergranular decohesion.
critiques.feasibility: High strain-rate testing methods (e.g., split-Hopkinson bar) and post-mortem microscopic analyses are well established, making this direction experimentally feasible.
critiques.evidence: While there is general literature on adiabatic shear bands in various systems, no specific prior records have been provided that directly support or contradict this mechanism.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the high strain-rate conditions might produce multiple overlapping deformation mechanisms, making it difficult to isolate the effect of localized adiabatic heating at grain boundaries.
critiques.fix: Refine the experimental design to better isolate the role of adiabatic heating—for example, by incorporating in situ temperature measurements and using additional strain-rate intervals to decouple overlapping effects.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction targets the open question by testing whether thermally induced nanoscale solute clustering at grain boundaries can reduce intergranular cohesion in HEAs, a mechanism distinct from coarse precipitation in conventional alloys.
critiques.constraints: It respects the imposed constraints by working with a single-phase equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA and controlling the thermal treatment to avoid unwanted grain growth or bulk phase transformations.
critiques.physical_soundness: The underlying concept of nanocluster formation at grain boundaries under intermediate aging conditions is physically plausible, though kinetic factors in HEAs may differ from conventional systems.
critiques.feasibility: Aging experiments and subsequent tensile tests, along with atom probe tomography and microscopy to detect nanoscale clustering, are all established procedures.
critiques.evidence: Although prior literature on subtle solute clustering in HEAs exists, no specific record IDs were provided to confirm or refute the approach.
critiques.main_risk: The primary risk is that the thermal treatments might inadvertently lead to larger-scale precipitate formation or grain coarsening, thereby confounding the intended test of subtle nanoclustering.
critiques.fix: Optimize the aging time–temperature parameters and introduce real-time characterization (e.g., in situ diffraction or small‐angle scattering) to ensure the evolution of only nanoclusters without triggering broader phase changes.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction explores a hypothesis that local chemical ordering (incipient intermetallic-like ordering) at grain boundaries can induce brittleness in HEAs, potentially offering a distinct mechanistic explanation from classical precipitation.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the constraints by maintaining single-phase FCC Al0.3CoCrFeNi under controlled annealing conditions designed to avoid global phase separation or significant grain growth.
critiques.physical_soundness: The hypothesis is physically plausible in that local ordering phenomena have been observed in complex alloys, though the sensitivity of detection and control over short-range order can be challenging.
critiques.feasibility: The proposed annealing treatments and high-resolution TEM/diffraction analyses are feasible with current methodologies, though sufficient resolution is required to detect the subtle features.
critiques.evidence: There is supportive literature on local ordering in similar alloy systems, but no specific record IDs were furnished to bolster this direction.
critiques.main_risk: A significant risk is that the processing window for inducing only local ordering at GBs without triggering coarser phase transformations is very narrow, making the observed effects difficult to reproduce.
critiques.fix: Incorporate complementary techniques such as atom probe tomography to cross-verify the presence of ordering, and conduct a systematic study of annealing times and temperatures to precisely map the narrow processing window.

critiques.addresses_problem: This approach examines whether trace impurity (oxygen) segregation at the grain boundaries can lead to brittle behavior in a HEA, invoking a mechanism similar to that in conventional alloys.
critiques.constraints: It meets the constraints by using a compositional complex HEA system (AlCoCrFeNiMo0.25) and maintaining a single-phase microstructure, although it intentionally introduces impurities.
critiques.physical_soundness: The concept of impurity-induced grain boundary decohesion is physically sound and well-documented in other alloy systems, but its relevance in HEAs—known for their impurity tolerance—remains less certain.
critiques.feasibility: The production of high-purity and intentionally doped alloys and the subsequent mechanical testing are both achievable with established methods.
critiques.evidence: There is broad literature on impurity-induced embrittlement, but no specific record IDs have been provided that attest to this effect in HEAs specifically.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the impurity mechanism may not be sufficiently dominant or may confound the intrinsic toughening mechanisms of HEAs, making it difficult to discern if any observed embrittlement is due solely to impurities.
critiques.fix: Establish more rigorous microanalytical characterization (e.g., using high-resolution EDS or atom probe tomography) to clearly isolate and quantify impurity segregation effects and ensure that observed embrittlement is not due to other processing artifacts.

decision.rationale: Direction B directly targets the open question by testing whether intermediate-temperature aging induces nanoclusters of solute elements (notably Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries, which in turn lower GB cohesion and lead to brittle behavior. This mechanism is distinct from the conventional precipitation route seen in traditional alloys. Although the initial proposal is viable, the critic’s suggestion to optimize aging parameters and to incorporate in situ or real‐time characterization (e.g., diffraction or small‐angle scattering) will help ensure that the treatment selectively induces nanoclustering without triggering unwanted grain coarsening or bulk phase separation. These modifications make this approach the most compelling given the supporting evidence from prior studies on nanocluster-induced embrittlement in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
